In the diagram, line [MATH: a] is parallel to line [MATH: b,] and line [MATH: t] intersects both lines. If [MATH: y = 4x + 3,] what is the value of [MATH: x?]

sections.normalized_html:
Since lines [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are parallel, and the line [MATH: t] acts as a transversal, the angle labeled [MATH: 69^\circ] and the angle adjacent to [MATH: y^\circ] inside the parallel lines are corresponding angles. Hence, they are congruent.

The angle labeled [MATH: y^\circ] and the adjacent angle form a linear pair, creating a straight angle at the point of intersection of [MATH: b] and [MATH: t.] The measure of a straight angle is [MATH: 180^\circ,] so we can write

[MATH: y^\circ + 69^\circ = 180^\circ.]

We are also told that [MATH: y = 4x + 3.] Substituting this and solving for [MATH: x,] we conclude that

[MATH: (4x + 3)^{∘} + 69^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 4x + 3 + 69|= 180; 4x + 72|= 180; 4x|= 108; x|= 27.]

sections.normalized_html: In the diagram above, lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel, [MATH: r = 50,] and [MATH: s = 60.] What is the value of [MATH: x]?
sections.readable_text:
[IMG: /graphics/d2c62b89ca066d9840291ed8e2579064]

In the diagram above, lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel, [MATH: r = 50,] and [MATH: s = 60.] What is the value of [MATH: x]?

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the triangle, shown in blue below, formed by the two non-parallel lines and the line [MATH: m.] Let [MATH: t^\circ] be the measure of the third angle of this triangle.

Note that, except for the side that is contained in the line [MATH: m,] the sides of the triangle act as transversals to the lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n.] Therefore, the angles whose measures are [MATH: s^\circ] and [MATH: t^\circ] are corresponding.

We are given that [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel. When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, corresponding angles are congruent. Therefore, [MATH: t^\circ = s^\circ.]

In any triangle, the sum of the measures of its interior angles is [MATH: 180^\circ.] So, we have [MATH: x^\circ + r^\circ + t^\circ = 180^\circ.] Substituting in the known values, we have [MATH: x^{∘} + 50^{∘} + 60^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; x^{∘} + 110^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; x^{∘}|= 70^{∘}.]

Therefore, we can conclude that [MATH: x = 70.]

2. [MATH: a + b > 180]
3. [MATH: b > 75]

sections.normalized_html:
Since lines [MATH: p] and [MATH: q] are parallel, and the line [MATH: t] acts as a transversal, the angle labeled [MATH: a^\circ] and the angle adjacent to [MATH: b^\circ] outside the parallel lines are corresponding angles. Hence, they are congruent.

The angle labeled [MATH: a^\circ] and the adjacent angle form a linear pair, creating a straight angle at the point of intersection of [MATH: t] and [MATH: q.] The measure of a straight angle is [MATH: 180^\circ,] so we can write

[MATH: b + a = 180.]

So, statement II is false.

Next, we are told that [MATH: a > 105.] Substituting this into the equation, we get [MATH: a|> 105; b + a|> b + 105; 180|> b + 105; 75|> b; b|< 75.]

So, statement I is true while statement III is false.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

sections.normalized_html: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the obtuse angles is [MATH: (11m + 94)^\circ.] The sum of one obtuse angle and three of the acute angles is [MATH: (k - 22m)^\circ.] What is the value of [MATH: k?]
sections.readable_text: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the obtuse angles is [MATH: (11m + 94)^\circ.] The sum of one obtuse angle and three of the acute angles is [MATH: (k - 22m)^\circ.] What is the value of [MATH: k?]

sections.normalized_html:
When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, it creates eight angles in total: four acute angles and four obtuse angles. All acute angles are congruent, and all obtuse angles are congruent, as shown below.

Let [MATH: \angle A] be an acute angle and [MATH: \angle O] be an obtuse angle.

In our case, the measure of one obtuse angle is [MATH: m\angle O = (11m + 94)^\circ.] Since acute and obtuse angles formed in this configuration are supplementary, their measures sum to [MATH: 180^\circ{:}]

[MATH: m\angle A + m\angle O = 180^\circ]

Hence, the measure of each acute angle is

[MATH: m∠A|= 180^{∘} − m∠O; = 180^{∘} − (11m + 94)^{∘}; = 180^{∘} − 11m^{∘} − 94^{∘}; = (86 − 11m)^{∘}.]

We are told that the sum of one obtuse angle and three acute angles is [MATH: (k - 22m)^\circ.] Writing as an equation, we have

[MATH: m\angle O + 3 \cdot m\angle A = (k - 22m)^\circ.]

Substituting in our expressions for [MATH: m\angle O] and [MATH: m\angle A,] we solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: (11m + 94)^{∘} + 3 ⋅ (86 − 11m)^{∘}|= (k − 22m)^{∘}; 11m + 94 + 258 − 33m|= k − 22m; 352 − 22m|= k − 22m; k|= 352]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
On the math section of the SAT exam, corresponding angles often appear in multi-step geometry problems involving parallel lines, transversals, and algebraic expressions.

Content:
Practicing how to connect these relationships, especially when they combine with supplementary or triangle angle rules, will help us solve geometry problems efficiently.

Item 2 — Example: Using Corresponding and Supplementary Angles

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/dea8036fb73d245d9715d2dbb09f1af2]

In the diagram, line [MATH: a] is parallel to line [MATH: b,] and line [MATH: t] intersects both lines. If [MATH: y = 4x + 3,] what is the value of [MATH: x?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since lines [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are parallel, and the line [MATH: t] acts as a transversal, the angle labeled [MATH: 69^\circ] and the angle adjacent to [MATH: y^\circ] inside the parallel lines are corresponding angles. Hence, they are congruent.

[IMG: /graphics/754c31781ca77cc771d022922c6e7e78]

The angle labeled [MATH: y^\circ] and the adjacent angle form a linear pair, creating a straight angle at the point of intersection of [MATH: b] and [MATH: t.] The measure of a straight angle is [MATH: 180^\circ,] so we can write

[MATH: y^\circ + 69^\circ = 180^\circ.]

We are also told that [MATH: y = 4x + 3.] Substituting this and solving for [MATH: x,] we conclude that

[MATH: (4x + 3)^{∘} + 69^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; 4x + 3 + 69|= 180; 4x + 72|= 180; 4x|= 108; x|= 27.]

Item 5 — Example: Using Corresponding Angles in Triangles

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/d2c62b89ca066d9840291ed8e2579064]

In the diagram above, lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel, [MATH: r = 50,] and [MATH: s = 60.] What is the value of [MATH: x]?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Consider the triangle, shown in blue below, formed by the two non-parallel lines and the line [MATH: m.] Let [MATH: t^\circ] be the measure of the third angle of this triangle.

[IMG: /graphics/dfca879119cfc6e20f8a767ad5ba4f19]

Note that, except for the side that is contained in the line [MATH: m,] the sides of the triangle act as transversals to the lines [MATH: m] and [MATH: n.] Therefore, the angles whose measures are [MATH: s^\circ] and [MATH: t^\circ] are corresponding.

We are given that [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are parallel. When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, corresponding angles are congruent. Therefore, [MATH: t^\circ = s^\circ.]

[IMG: /graphics/a5b744b6209161453449aa4d7f18f149]

In any triangle, the sum of the measures of its interior angles is [MATH: 180^\circ.] So, we have
[MATH: x^\circ + r^\circ + t^\circ = 180^\circ.]
Substituting in the known values, we have
[MATH: x^{∘} + 50^{∘} + 60^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; x^{∘} + 110^{∘}|= 180^{∘}; x^{∘}|= 70^{∘}.]

Therefore, we can conclude that [MATH: x = 70.]

Item 8 — Example: Using Corresponding and Supplementary Angles With Inequalities

Example Prompt:
[IMG: /graphics/69ca499a6e4392c3dee330e4ee7c882d]

In the diagram above, lines [MATH: p] and [MATH: q] are parallel, and the line [MATH: t] intersects both. If [MATH: a > 105,] which of the following must be true?

1. [MATH: b < 75]
2. [MATH: a + b > 180]
3. [MATH: b > 75]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since lines [MATH: p] and [MATH: q] are parallel, and the line [MATH: t] acts as a transversal, the angle labeled [MATH: a^\circ] and the angle adjacent to [MATH: b^\circ] outside the parallel lines are corresponding angles. Hence, they are congruent.

[IMG: /graphics/39dcbe9c54a7b59369ab33858b5fd89a]

The angle labeled [MATH: a^\circ] and the adjacent angle form a linear pair, creating a straight angle at the point of intersection of [MATH: t] and [MATH: q.] The measure of a straight angle is [MATH: 180^\circ,] so we can write

[MATH: b + a = 180.]

So, statement II is false.

Next, we are told that [MATH: a > 105.] Substituting this into the equation, we get
[MATH: a|> 105; b + a|> b + 105; 180|> b + 105; 75|> b; b|< 75.]

So, statement I is true while statement III is false.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

Item 11 — Example: Finding an Unknown Constant Given Expressions for Supplementary Angles

Example Prompt:
A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the obtuse angles is [MATH: (11m + 94)^\circ.] The sum of one obtuse angle and three of the acute angles is [MATH: (k - 22m)^\circ.] What is the value of [MATH: k?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
When a transversal intersects two parallel lines, it creates eight angles in total: four acute angles and four obtuse angles. All acute angles are congruent, and all obtuse angles are congruent, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/473f35fb33db4090d0063c6e62ff37c5]

Let [MATH: \angle A] be an acute angle and [MATH: \angle O] be an obtuse angle.

In our case, the measure of one obtuse angle is [MATH: m\angle O = (11m + 94)^\circ.] Since acute and obtuse angles formed in this configuration are supplementary, their measures sum to [MATH: 180^\circ{:}]

[MATH: m\angle A + m\angle O = 180^\circ]

Hence, the measure of each acute angle is

[MATH: m∠A|= 180^{∘} − m∠O; = 180^{∘} − (11m + 94)^{∘}; = 180^{∘} − 11m^{∘} − 94^{∘}; = (86 − 11m)^{∘}.]

We are told that the sum of one obtuse angle and three acute angles is [MATH: (k - 22m)^\circ.] Writing as an equation, we have

[MATH: m\angle O + 3 \cdot m\angle A = (k - 22m)^\circ.]

Substituting in our expressions for [MATH: m\angle O] and [MATH: m\angle A,] we solve for [MATH: k,] as follows:

[MATH: (11m + 94)^{∘} + 3 ⋅ (86 − 11m)^{∘}|= (k − 22m)^{∘}; 11m + 94 + 258 − 33m|= k − 22m; 352 − 22m|= k − 22m; k|= 352]
